generalMobility.source: Konrad et al. (2024), Journal of Sport and Health Science, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37301370/ (general chronic stretching ROM evidence; not muscle-specific superiority)
generalMobility.static: 20–30 seconds x 2 as practical default, 3–5 days/week if needed
generalMobility.pnf: Optional gentle contraction 5–10 seconds then 15–30 seconds stretch, not necessary or proven superior for these muscles
generalMobility.evidence: Strong general ROM evidence; specific doses and stretches Limited; no guaranteed soreness or injury benefit

hip flexors.rom: Hip extension lengthens iliopsoas; no verified lengthened-partial growth comparison.
hip flexors.mobility: Half-kneeling hip-flexor stretch with gentle posterior pelvic tilt; 2 x 20–30 s.
hip flexors.warmup: Unloaded marches, then light band hip flexion.
hip flexors.limits: Power and hypertrophy rankings indirect; healthy young adult strength RCT.
hip flexors.source: Thorborg et al. (2016), Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00167-015-3583-y (healthy adult band hip-flexion RCT; strength only)

rotator cuff.rom: Use controlled comfortable rotation; no proven lengthened partial advantage.
rotator cuff.mobility: Gentle cross-body shoulder stretch if restricted; avoid forcing rotation.
rotator cuff.warmup: Light external/internal rotation and task-specific press ramp-up.
rotator cuff.limits: EMG is recruitment only; shoulder prevention programmes have conflicting findings.
rotator cuff.source: Reinold et al. (2004), Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15296366/ (acute EMG, not growth or prevention); Andersson et al. (2017), British Journal of Sports Medicine, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27313171/ (multicomponent handball programme, not isolated exercise); 2025 review https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41035524/ found no significant pooled benefit

serratus anterior.rom: Allow natural protraction/upward rotation; no comparative growth ROM trial verified.
serratus anterior.mobility: Comfortable overhead reach and thoracic rotation, not a proven isolated serratus stretch.
serratus anterior.warmup: Wall push-up plus, then task-specific ramp-up.
serratus anterior.limits: Activation evidence only; no isolated power or injury-prevention claim.
serratus anterior.source: Kang et al. (2019), Journal of Athletic Training, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31584855/ (EMG systematic review, not injury outcomes)

tibialis anterior.rom: Comfortable plantarflexion to dorsiflexion; no verified lengthened partial trial.
tibialis anterior.mobility: Gentle seated plantarflexion stretch if needed; no forced kneeling.
tibialis anterior.limits: No verified isolated hypertrophy or shin-splint prevention trial.
tibialis anterior.source: Currier et al. (2026), Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897 (general resistance training; indirect)

foot intrinsic muscles.rom: Controlled toe and arch movement; no established optimal lengthened load.
foot intrinsic muscles.mobility: Gentle toe extension and active toe spreading; no forced arch stretch.
foot intrinsic muscles.warmup: Seated short-foot practice before standing balance.
foot intrinsic muscles.limits: Reviews support function; injury prevention and isolated power remain unproven.
foot intrinsic muscles.source: Jaffri et al. (2023), Journal of Athletic Training, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35724360/ (foot function systematic review; mixed populations)

ankle invertors.rom: Comfortable inversion/eversion; no forced end-range loading.
ankle invertors.mobility: Active ankle circles; gentle eversion if restricted.
ankle invertors.limits: Balance programme evidence does not establish isolated invertor prevention.
ankle invertors.source: Schiftan et al. (2015), Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24831756/ (proprioceptive training, particularly recurrent ankle sprains; not isolated strengthening)

ankle evertors.mobility: Active ankle circles; gentle inversion only if comfortable.
ankle evertors.warmup: Light band eversion and single-leg balance.
ankle evertors.limits: Recurrent sprain prevention is programme-level; isolated power unverified.
ankle evertors.source: Schiftan et al. (2015), Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24831756/ (proprioceptive training, particularly recurrent ankle sprains; not isolated strengthening)

hip external rotators.rom: Rotation range depends on hip position and anatomy; no comparative hypertrophy evidence.
hip external rotators.mobility: Supported 90/90 position or gentle figure-four stretch, 2 x 20–30 s.
hip external rotators.warmup: Active hip rotations and light clamshells.
hip external rotators.limits: Clinical hip programmes are not proof of healthy-athlete injury prevention.
hip external rotators.source: Currier et al. (2026), Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897 (general resistance training; indirect)

hip internal rotators.rom: Use comfortable rotation; no forced end range or lengthened partial evidence.
hip internal rotators.limits: No verified isolated hypertrophy, power or injury prevention trials.
hip internal rotators.source: Currier et al. (2026), Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000003897 (general resistance training; indirect)

quadratus lumborum.rom: Controlled lateral flexion and anti-lateral flexion; no verified long-length hypertrophy comparison.
quadratus lumborum.mobility: Gentle standing side reach, 2 x 20–30 s.
quadratus lumborum.warmup: Easy side plank or unloaded side bends.
quadratus lumborum.limits: EMG in healthy men only; side plank is not established as best for growth.
quadratus lumborum.source: Oshikawa et al. (2020), Journal of Sport Rehabilitation, https://doi.org/10.1123/jsr.2019-0225 (acute EMG in 13 healthy men)

diaphragm.rom: Respiratory excursion is not gym joint ROM; no stretch-mediated hypertrophy prescription.
diaphragm.mobility: Relaxed breathing; no static/PNF stretching target.
diaphragm.limits: Device protocols often use 30 breaths once or twice daily; actual resistance and frequency individualised; no universal sports performance benefit.
diaphragm.source: Illi et al. (2012), Sports Medicine, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22765281/ (respiratory training meta-analysis; endurance outcomes)

pelvic floor.rom: Contraction and full relaxation, not forced stretching or loaded partials.
pelvic floor.mobility: Relaxed breathing and clinician-guided relaxation if indicated; no routine stretching target.
pelvic floor.limits: Clinical female incontinence evidence; no automatic prescription for healthy users, pain or hypertonicity; clinician sets dose.
pelvic floor.source: Dumoulin et al. (2018), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD005654.pub4 (women with urinary incontinence; not universal prevention)

drills.name: Pelvic floor relaxation with breathing
drills.note: Specialist only: relaxation awareness, not proven treatment or flexibility gain; avoid straining; seek pelvic health clinician for pain, urgency or leakage.
drills.source: Dumoulin et al. (2018), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD005654.pub4 (women with urinary incontinence; not universal prevention)

drills.name: Half-kneeling hip-flexor stretch with gentle posterior pelvic tilt
drills.note: Half-kneeling hip-flexor stretch with gentle posterior pelvic tilt; 2 x 20–30 s. General static stretching and PNF can increase ROM; dynamic movement for warm-up. Specific superiority and injury/soreness reduction not established. Hip extension lengthens iliopsoas; no verified lengthened-partial growth comparison. For flexibility practice 3–5 days/week as needed; static holds 20–30 seconds, 2 sets; active drills 5–10 reps. Dose is a practical default.
drills.source: Konrad et al. (2024), Journal of Sport and Health Science, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37301370/ (general chronic stretching ROM evidence; not muscle-specific superiority)

drills.name: Gentle cross-body shoulder stretch if restricted
drills.note: Gentle cross-body shoulder stretch if restricted; avoid forcing rotation. General static stretching and PNF can increase ROM; dynamic movement for warm-up. Specific superiority and injury/soreness reduction not established. Use controlled comfortable rotation; no proven lengthened partial advantage. For flexibility practice 3–5 days/week as needed; static holds 20–30 seconds, 2 sets; active drills 5–10 reps. Dose is a practical default.
drills.source: Konrad et al. (2024), Journal of Sport and Health Science, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37301370/ (general chronic stretching ROM evidence; not muscle-specific superiority)

drills.name: Comfortable overhead reach and thoracic rotation, not a proven isolated serratus stretch.
drills.note: Comfortable overhead reach and thoracic rotation, not a proven isolated serratus stretch. General static stretching and PNF can increase ROM; dynamic movement for warm-up. Specific superiority and injury/soreness reduction not established. Allow natural protraction/upward rotation; no comparative growth ROM trial verified. For flexibility practice 3–5 days/week as needed; static holds 20–30 seconds, 2 sets; active drills 5–10 reps. Dose is a practical default.
drills.source: Konrad et al. (2024), Journal of Sport and Health Science, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37301370/ (general chronic stretching ROM evidence; not muscle-specific superiority)

drills.note: Gentle seated plantarflexion stretch if needed; no forced kneeling. General static stretching and PNF can increase ROM; dynamic movement for warm-up. For flexibility practice 3–5 days/week as needed; static holds 20–30 seconds, 2 sets; active drills 5–10 reps. Dose is a practical default.
drills.source: Konrad et al. (2024), Journal of Sport and Health Science, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37301370/ (general chronic stretching ROM evidence; not muscle-specific superiority)

For flexibility practice 3–5 days/week as needed; static holds 20–30 seconds, 2 sets; active drills 5–10 reps. Dose is a practical default.
